title: CHAPTER 6: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS AND LABOUR LAWS

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Industrial Relations establishes the core concepts and fundamental importance of managing employee-employer dynamics.
Trade Unions in India function as organized bodies representing labor interests and negotiating workplace terms.
Collective Bargaining and its structured process serve as primary mechanisms for reaching mutual agreements.
The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 serves as the legal backbone for preventing and settling industrial conflicts in India.
Standardized Grievance Handling Procedures and Domestic Enquiries ensure procedural fairness and discipline in the workplace.

blocks.content: Industrial Relations (IR) refers to the complex of interrelations among workers, managers, and government. It encompasses all aspects of the employment relationship :wages, working conditions, discipline, welfare, union-management relations, and collective bargaining.

cells: Management and workers share same goals; conflict is deviant; unions are unnecessary
Harmony natural; effective management prevents conflict; paternalistic
Multiple groups with legitimate interests; conflict natural; managed through negotiation and institutions
Conflict accepted; collective bargaining; welfare state approach; most mainstream HR perspective
Fundamental conflict between capital and labour; unions as instruments of class struggle; system change needed
Capitalism inherently exploitative; IR is expression of class conflict
IR as a system with actors (workers, managers, government), contexts (technology, market, power), and outputs (rules)
IR rules are outputs of a system; study actors, contexts, and ideology binding them

blocks.content: A trade union is an organisation of workers formed to protect and promote their interests in relation to wages, working conditions, security of employment, and other matters. Trade Union Act, 1926 governs registration and protection of trade unions in India.

cells: Registration with Registrar of Trade Unions; registered TU gets legal entity; minimum 7 members needed for registration
Immunity from civil suits for acts in contemplation of trade disputes; right to negotiate; right to representation; right to collect subscriptions
No compulsory recognition law in India; TNRB (Trade Union Recognition Bill) pending; voluntary recognition by management
Deduction of union subscription from wages by employer and remittance to union; written consent of member required
India has multiple unions in same enterprise; lack of one single representative union; weakness of union movement
Trade Union Act allows outsiders (politicians, professionals) to be office bearers of TU; controversial; politicisation of unions
INTUC (INC), AITUC (CPI), CITU (CPM), BMS (RSS/BJP), HMS, UTUC, AIUTUC, TUCC, SEWA (unorganised sector women)
AIBEA (All India Bank Employees' Association); AIBOA; INBEF; NOBW; BEFI; NCBE :multiple unions in banking sector

blocks.content: CHAPTER 6: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS AND LABOUR LAWS

Collective Bargaining is a process of negotiation between employers and a group of employees (usually represented by a trade union) to determine employment terms. It aims to reach a collective agreement or settlement.

cells: Win-lose; fixed pie; one side's gain is the other's loss; wage negotiations; zero-sum game
Win-win; expand the pie; mutual gain; interest-based; long-term relationship focus
Union makes concessions to management; givebacks; during financial crisis or to save jobs
Management offers higher wages in exchange for work practice changes; increased efficiency commitment

items: Step 1: Preparation :both parties research positions; analyse data; set objectives; identify priorities
Step 2: Opening :each party presents initial demands; position statements; anchoring
Step 3: Bargaining :exchange proposals; make concessions; find zones of agreement; deadlines create pressure
Step 4: Agreement :draft settlement; review; sign collective agreement/bipartite settlement
Step 5: Implementation :communicate to all employees; monitor compliance; handle disputes on interpretation

cells: Any dispute between employer-employer, employer-workmen, workmen-workmen related to employment, non-employment, terms of employment, or conditions of labour
Employed for hire/reward for manual/skilled/unskilled/technical/operational/clerical/supervisory work; not managerial, administrative, supervisory earning >Rs.10,000 (pre-amendment)
Any business, trade, undertaking, manufacture, calling; includes service organisations; Bangalore Water Supply Case (1978) broad interpretation
Appointed by Government to mediate disputes; investigates and mediates; files failure report if settlement not reached
For important disputes; tripartite board; temporary body
Investigates causes of dispute; report to Government; no binding award
Adjudicates discharge/dismissal disputes, interpretation of awards; one presiding officer
Broader jurisdiction including wages, conditions; presiding officer with HC judge qualification
For national importance disputes; appointed by Central Government
Cessation of work by body of employees acting in combination; go-slow is not strike but unfair practice
Temporary closure of place of employment or suspension of work by employer
6 weeks notice for public utility services; not during conciliation/arbitration proceedings
Failure/inability of employer to provide employment due to shortage of material, power, natural calamity
50% of basic wages + DA for laid-off workmen (not casual/badli workers)
Termination of service for any reason except dismissal/retirement/non-renewal of fixed-term contract/voluntary retirement/continued ill health
1 month notice or pay in lieu; 15 days wages per year of service as compensation; prior government permission for 100+ workers
Workmen protected if undertaking transferred; new employer bound by service conditions

blocks.content: A grievance is any dissatisfaction or feeling of injustice in connection with one's employment situation. Effective grievance handling prevents small issues from escalating into industrial disputes.

items: High exam relevance: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provisions, dispute settlement machinery, and statutory definitions.
Sequence of steps in the Collective Bargaining Process and Model Grievance Handling Procedure are frequently asked in objective exams.
Key questions often focus on principles of Natural Justice applicable during Discipline and Domestic Enquiry.

cells: Employee presents grievance; supervisor responds; informal resolution
If unresolved, HR Manager and Departmental Head examine and respond
Grievance Committee with union representation if any; formal hearing; written decision
If still unresolved, refer to Labour Court, Tribunal, or Arbitration (if agreed)
Create environment where employees voluntarily follow rules; training; clear communication; fair treatment
Punishment for violations; progressive discipline: oral warning → written warning → suspension → dismissal
Breach of employer's rules and regulations; may be minor (casual leave abuse) or major (fraud, assault, insubordination)
Internal investigation before imposing major punishment; principles of natural justice must be followed
Audi alteram partem (hear both sides); Nemo judex in causa sua (unbiased enquiry officer); Reasoned order
First step in disciplinary process; employee asked to explain conduct; opportunity to defend before punishment
Specific charges framed against delinquent employee; basis of domestic enquiry
Independent officer; hears both sides; examines evidence; submits findings report
Dismissal, Removal, Compulsory Retirement, Reduction in rank, Withholding increment with cumulative effect
Censure, Withholding increment (non-cumulative), Recovery of loss from salary, Withholding promotion
Order of Supreme Court (ECIL v. B. Karunakar, 1993)
Employee must be provided copy of enquiry report before final punishment order; opportunity to make representation
